metadata.title: A Fixed-Domain Exhaustion Theorem Standing, Consequence, and Compositional Closure
metadata.description:
A Fixed-Domain Exhaustion Theorem

Standing, Consequence, and Compositional Closure

Overview

This paper develops a fixed-domain exhaustion theorem for admissible descriptions, representations, interfaces, continuations, and authorization systems.

A record may give the correct verdict while omitting evidence required by the original protocol. Two inputs may receive the same present answer while differing in whether a future operation is safe or authorized. A proposed interface may preserve all observed results while failing to preserve a required continuation, certificate, history, or joint-use condition.

The paper asks what it means for a representation to preserve every use of an independently specified task.

The answer is obtained by fixing the original bearer, questions, answer meanings, continuation requirements, support obligations, and authorization rules before evaluating the proposed realization.

Complete original profiles

The paper begins with an independently specified family of original questions. Each question has:

  • a bearer;

  • an occurrence or context;

  • a required use;

  • a value space;

  • a partial answer relation;

  • an explicit distinction between an undefined answer and a negative answer.

The complete outcome profile records every original answer together with its definedness. This profile determines a canonical quotient of the original descriptions.

Descriptions are identified only when they agree on the complete original profile. If two descriptions agree on all currently observed values but differ under a required continuation, they remain distinct in the complete quotient.

This distinguishes:

  • present observational agreement;

  • complete behavioural equivalence;

  • future-use equivalence;

  • historical identity;

  • physical or mathematical realization.

Canonical quotient and minimal complete interface

The paper proves that the complete outcome profile determines a unique minimal complete quotient, up to the unique commuting bijection.

Every complete interface must determine this quotient. If an interface merges two descriptions that differ on an original question, then there is a witness showing that the interface cannot answer that question correctly for both inputs.

A proposed interface can therefore fail in two different ways:

  • it can lose information required by the original task;

  • it can retain sufficient information but apply an incorrect reader or interpretation.

The quotient theorem separates these failures. A collision in the retained code is an information failure; an incorrect reported result is a graph or interpretation failure.

Generated uses and compositional exhaustion

For deterministic partial operations, the paper characterizes exactly when a quotient preserves all finite observations generated by the available operations.

The central condition is descent:

  • the operation domain must be saturated on the proposed equivalence classes;

  • equivalent inputs must produce equivalent outputs wherever the operation is defined;

  • definedness and failure behaviour must be preserved;

  • finite compositions must remain interpretable in the retained language.

Primitive descent extends through finite words and strict finite constructor trees. Conversely, a failure of primitive descent supplies a finite mismatch witness.

The paper distinguishes determination by the complete observation profile from expression by finitely many observations. A result may be determined by the entire profile while no finite prefix or finite expression is sufficient to decide it.

Fixed-domain safe interior

For an independently specified reuse contract, the paper constructs the unique greatest complete safe interior.

A safe interior must:

  • include every state satisfying the declared local conditions;

  • exclude every state from which an unsafe continuation is reachable;

  • preserve the original node and edge conditions;

  • remain closed under the permitted updates;

  • retain the stated interpretation of reuse and authorization.

An included unsafe state supplies a finite path witnessing failure. An omitted safe state supplies a sound region witnessing incomplete coverage.

The theorem therefore distinguishes:

  • a false safe-region claim;

  • a sound but incomplete safe region;

  • a complete safe region;

  • a region whose safety depends on an unstated change of contract.

Exhaustion of result, information, continuation, and support obligations

The fixed-domain exhaustion theorem gives a witness for every way in which a claimed complete realization can fail.

The failure classes include:

  • an incorrect result;

  • an omitted required result;

  • a retained code that merges distinguishable inputs;

  • a failure to preserve definedness;

  • a failure to preserve a continuation;

  • an unsafe included state;

  • an omitted safe state;

  • a missing certificate;

  • an invalid or ungrounded certificate;

  • an unsupported interpretation;

  • a failure of joint compatibility;

  • a failure of sequential authorization;

  • an incorrect rejection reason;

  • an unpreserved historical distinction.

The last class is important: a conclusion can be true while the required certificate or support obligation remains unfulfilled. Truth of the conclusion does not automatically discharge the obligation to provide the warranted support.

History and irreversible retention

The paper treats history as part of the original task whenever the task asks about an occurrence, prior failure, sequence of operations, or retained commitment.

A repaired system can pass a new trial without erasing the earlier failure. A new positive endpoint can coexist with a retained negative historical record.

The theorem therefore distinguishes:

  • repair of a later state;

  • replacement by a new occurrence;

  • correction of a faulty record;

  • preservation of the original history;

  • absorption or erasure of an earlier failure.

Faithful redescription cannot remove a witnessed historical distinction when that distinction belongs to the original question set.

Grounded authorization

The paper also studies extensions of a rule system and asks when they preserve the original authorization judgments.

An extension preserves old authorization only when it:

  • retains the original warranted entrances;

  • retains the original rules;

  • preserves the original derivations;

  • does not create new derivations of previously unsupported original claims;

  • preserves the interpretation of the original vocabulary.

This separates grounded authorization from mere closure. A mutually supporting cycle can be closed under its rules while remaining ungrounded if no independently warranted entrance reaches it.

The result applies to proof systems, admissibility systems, certification records, and any construction where conclusions require support rather than truth alone.

Consequence determination and uniqueness

The paper distinguishes several forms of uniqueness:

  • unique output for a fixed input;

  • a common output across a candidate family;

  • a unique occupant compatible with a readout;

  • a unique normal form;

  • a unique decomposition;

  • a unique realization.

A unique output across a candidate family requires a nonempty singleton readout image. A unique occupant requires a singleton identity image over the observed readout. A unique decomposition requires a singleton assembly fibre.

Determinacy of each individual input is not enough to establish uniqueness across a family. Likewise, a specified codomain or one-bit qualification does not by itself select a unique mechanism, occupant, or decomposition.

Joint compatibility and compositional closure

The paper shows why individually qualified components may fail to form an admissible composite.

Two components can each satisfy the same unary qualification while their joint tuple differs in compatibility. A proposed constructor must therefore preserve:

  • the joint domain;

  • the compatibility relation;

  • retained outputs;

  • failure behaviour;

  • authorization at every construction node.

For finite assembly trees, primitive joint descent extends compositionally once these conditions are established at each constructor.

This provides an exact test for when independent component descriptions can be safely combined.

Worked constructions

The paper includes worked examples involving:

  • bridge trials and repeat-use behaviour;

  • binary qualification and multi-class behaviour;

  • joint compatibility missed by unary inspection;

  • typed lambda-calculus constructions;

  • preservation versus evaluation success;

  • unique-output claims requiring an additional domain theorem;

  • finite formation and eventual-outcome questions;

  • safe interiors and invariant regions;

  • certificate delivery and support obligations;

  • historical retention after repair;

  • quotient factorization and output uniqueness;

  • ungrounded authorization cycles.

These examples show that the theorem’s distinctions are not terminological. Each one corresponds to a concrete separating model or failure witness.

Relation to AASC

The Kernel result supplies the necessary roles of Admissibility, Standing, Reference, and Irreversibility for non-degenerate determinate objects.

The AMetric Boundary develops pre-fixational authority, symmetry, and non-transmission. The Structure of Admissibility develops complete interfaces and the greatest admissible interior. The present paper supplies the generic original-task, profile, coverage, witness, history, support, and compositional-exhaustion results needed by downstream applications.

The AASC conclusion concerns determinate objects, records, states, carriers, and endpoints. It is not an optional downstream encoding rule.

At the same time, each application must independently specify:

  • the original bearer;

  • the original questions;

  • the answer meanings;

  • the reuse contract;

  • the authorization rules;

  • the required support;

  • the interpretation of each operation.

The exhaustion theorem tests a proposed realization relative to those meanings. It does not allow a later representation to redefine the original task in order to avoid a failure witness.

Formal verification

The accompanying project contains machine-checked proofs of selected results together with finite separating models and bounded verification checks.

The formal and computational record covers:

  • complete-profile reconstruction;

  • quotient and decoder properties;

  • finite continuation descent;

  • joint assembly compatibility;

  • greatest safe interiors;

  • certificate and support obligations;

  • grounded authorization;

  • consequence and occupant uniqueness;

  • decomposition uniqueness;

  • historical retention;

  • failure-witness construction.

The verification guide records the hypotheses represented in Lean and the declarations checked. The paper distinguishes these formal checks from the independent semantic work required to establish the original meaning of an application.

Scope and limitations

The paper establishes:

  • a canonical quotient from complete original profiles;

  • unique minimal complete interfaces;

  • finite-use and compositional descent criteria;

  • exact safe-interior construction;

  • witnessed exhaustion of incorrect or incomplete realizations;

  • support and certificate obligations;

  • historical retention under faithful redescription;

  • grounded authorization under conservative extension;

  • output, occupant, and decomposition uniqueness criteria;

  • joint compatibility and sequential authorization conditions;

  • faithful-redescription closure of failure witnesses.

It does not claim:

  • that every original question is decidable;

  • that every complete profile has a finite representation;

  • that every safe interior is inhabited;

  • that one qualification bit captures complete behaviour;

  • that a true conclusion discharges an absent support obligation;

  • that endpoint equality erases history;

  • that equal cardinalities establish a product decomposition;

  • that every candidate family has a unique occupant;

  • that a downstream representation can derive or replace the AASC Kernel.

The conclusions are relative to the independently specified original task, answer relations, continuation rules, support obligations, and authorization structure.

Place in the AASC archive

This paper is the general exhaustion and compositional-closure theorem underlying the AASC description, interface, and realization programme.
